page_title: Sapphire Rapids: Golden Cove Hits Servers

sources.entry: Sapphire Rapids: Golden Cove Hits Servers - Measures L3 and memory latency across the tiled mesh and the slow clock ramp the vendor overview omits.

summary.title: Sapphire Rapids: Golden Cove Hits Servers
summary.one_liner: Intel's Sapphire Rapids server chip has strong AVX-512/AMX vector hardware, but its tiled mesh gives it very high L3 latency and weak instruction fetch from L3 compared with AMD's Milan.
takeaways: Sapphire Rapids keeps two 512-bit FMA units and drops the fixed AVX-512 clock penalty seen on early chips, though clocks vary with turbo.
Its L2 grows to 2 MB with a 16-cycle latency, trading latency for capacity, as Intel tends to do.
L3 latency is very high (about 33 ns) because a large mesh connects 56 cores and 56 L3 slices across die boundaries, and it regressed about 33% from Ice Lake SP.
Per-core L3 bandwidth is similar to Ice Lake, and instruction fetch from L3 falls below 1 IPC, which may bottleneck large code footprints.
AMD's clustered L3 design and V-Cache offer better L3 performance, so Sapphire Rapids' advantages look narrow in the server market.
summary.summary: This Chips and Cheese article benchmarks Sapphire Rapids (Xeon Platinum 8480) on Intel DevCloud and Google Cloud, covering clock ramp, AVX-512 execution, register renaming, the cache hierarchy, and load/store behavior. It compares results against Golden Cove, Ice Lake SP, Zen 3, Milan EPYC parts, and Graviton 3 using latency and bandwidth tests. It also includes Minecraft server benchmarks run by a guest contributor. The author concludes that the large unified mesh gives Intel flexibility but high L3 latency, and that AMD's design has the stronger server advantage.
